question: A woman appears in consultation with her 3-year-old daughter because she has detected slight breast development for 3 months without taking medication or objectifying relevant history. Effectively, the physical examination shows a Tanner IV stage, without pubic or axillary hair growth. The external genitalia are normal. The ultrasound reveals a small uterus and radiology a bone age of 3 years. What attitude should be adopted?

options.opa: Follow-up every 3-4 months, since it is a temporary condition that often resolves itself.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Premature thelarche (isolated breast development in girls before the age of 8) -> Tanner IV stage breast development -> Normal external genitalia -> Small uterus on ultrasound -> Bone age of 3 years -> Possible follow-up every 3-4 months -> 70%

CHAIN: Premature thelarche -> Exclude other causes of early puberty (e.g., central precocious puberty) -> Normal pubic and axillary hair growth -> No signs of virilization -> No medication history -> No relevant family history -> Consider follow-up every 3-4 months -> 80%

CHAIN: Premature thelarche -> Rule out underlying pathology through history, physical examination, and investigations -> No signs of malignancy on examination -> No indication for breast biopsy or mammography -> Consider follow-up every 3-4 months -> 90%
